Proving Ground · the forward-looking instrument

A market for stories that don’t exist yet.

Proving Ground creates demand for scripts that have not been made. It renders unproduced scripts as 30-second trailers, puts them in front of fans, and measures what those fans do — not what they say. That demand is priced, sold to the people who fund production, and used for one purpose: getting the scripts fans want made.

Supply finds demand — an unmade script is read by the audience it was written for. Demand finds supply — what that audience does is priced and handed to the people who can make it. The demand data is the product; the produced script is the point.

1 · RenderA trailer from an unproduced script30 seconds, $2–11 a take, days not months.
2 · FansDemand is created and measuredWatch, replay, scroll-away, head-to-head — behaviour, not opinion.
3 · SellDemand data becomes a productCertificates, closed panels, a standing Demand Feed.
4 · ProduceThe script gets madeOption flow to buyers; writers produced, paid, acknowledged.

01 First principlesPost-mortems

Every demand signal the industry owns is a post-mortem.

Mara’s script has three readers’ praise and no signal. Every signal Mr. Biggles can pull up — box office, delivery, minutes — belongs to films that already exist. TIDELOCK does not.

Strip the industry to first principles and it has exactly two unsolved problems, and they are the same problem. Box office, Nielsen delivery, streaming minutes — every signal the industry owns measures things already written, already cast, already paid for.

Demand is read after release. Nothing the industry owns reads it before.

01 The one-line versionLoaded, defaults (E)

Proving Ground creates the demand, sells the data, and gets the script made.

It renders unmade scripts and concepts as watchable 30-second trailers, puts them in front of a live global audience, and converts what that audience watches, finishes, replays and ranks head-to-head into a priced demand signal — resolved against Shiv's Curated Content Catalog.

Three things follow, in order. Demand is created where none could exist before — fans discover a script through its trailer. The demand data is sold — to studios, streamers and buyers as certificates, panels and a standing feed. The script gets produced — the buyer who paid for the signal is the buyer who options it. Move the audience test from rough cut to first draft, drop the cost of asking by three orders of magnitude, and sell the answer to the people writing the cheques.

02 The gap§02 tiles

Two queues that never meet.

Supply sits at concept. Demand is read at rough cut and release, after the money. Nothing reads between them at first draft. Proving Ground reads here — on behaviour.

Short-form is where this starts, and the format is already being industrialised: micro-drama studios in China are replacing actors with AI to feed it. Proving Ground runs the other way. AI renders the trailer to find the audience; the audience's demand gets the human-written script produced. The output is not slop at scale — it is a produced title that fans asked for before anyone spent the money.

03 The loop behind the readInstrumented

Render → Vote → Resolve → Price. A certificate at the end.

Four stages, each instrumented. A script is rendered as a 30-second trailer; a live audience votes with behaviour — completion, replay, scroll-away, head-to-head; the concept is resolved against the Curated Content Catalog; the result is priced and signed.

The loop runs at first draft, in days, for cents a read. It does not end in a report: a priced concept leaves the loop toward a buyer, and the buyer's option is what turns demand into a produced title. The certificate is the product; production is the point.

Out of the drawer

The script leaves the drawer as a file. Before any vendor sees a page, the Gateway has redacted it and written the ledger row. Then the models take their seats.

04 Best-in-role · every seat swappableAs of Sep 2026

No single model runs this loop, and none of them is the product.

TIDELOCK enters as a file. One model breaks it into beats, another renders the tide, a third checks the take. None of them owns the script or the result.

No single model can run this loop well, so none is asked to. Each seat goes to the model that currently wins its bake-off, behind the Model Gateway — a provenance wall where a model earns production status and loses it the same way.

Named today, married never. The models are components; the spine, the telemetry and the certificates are the IP.

05 PrecedentTMDB · 14 released titles

The industry has measured demand before production exactly fourteen times that anyone remembers.

Mr. Biggles has sat through every one of these decks. Leaked test footage. A Kickstarter. A redesign after one trailer. Every one of those was an accident that worked.

Deadpool’s test footage leaked in 2014 and the studio greenlit a film it had shelved for years on the reaction. Veronica Mars was paid for by 91,000 fans before a frame was shot. Sonic was redrawn because a trailer told the studio what the audience would not accept. Paranormal Activity asked fans to vote for the cities it would open in.

Snakes on a Plane is on the shelf too: the loudest demand of its decade, and it underperformed. Loud is not deep, and an interval matters. The instrument’s job is to make the accident routine — and to say how sure it is.

Every circle is a script. Explore them the way an audience does — by feeling, not by genre.

05 The voteSimulated · uncalibrated

Seven seconds, one thumb, and the interval narrows.

Dani watches, slides, lets go. Mr. Biggles watches the ring move.

The workflow, once, end to end. The trailer plays for seven seconds. A slider appears; she pushes it to 74 and releases. The vote lands in the ring, and the ring is the only number a studio ever sees. Under it the interval narrows as reads arrive — ±14 points at 48 reads, ±2 at 2,000 — and the certificate is stamped.

Each stage writes a row to the ledger: play, complete, vote, certificate. The number is uncalibrated until 200 released titles have been read blind and the ring’s scale has been fitted to what they went on to earn. Until then the ring says so in its own label.

06 The calculatorMaths is live

Drag the sliders. The maths is live.

Renders per concept = 3 candidate takes + 1 QC-approved final = 4. Per take = seconds × rate. Loaded = (render + acquisition + opex) ÷ reads. Orders = log10($37.50 ÷ loaded).

At the defaults: $14.40 a concept, 2.72¢ a read, 1,378 reads for the price of one screening recruit — 3.1 orders of magnitude.

06 PrecisionArithmetic

What the audience size buys: the interval.

Precision is ±1.96·√(0.25/n). n=400 → ±4.9 pp; n=2,000 → ±2.2 pp; n=25,000 → ±0.6 pp. Arithmetic, not a claim.

One screening recruit is the orange square. For the same money the loaded read buys the cyan cloud — and the narrower interval that comes with it.

The comparable

One vote is a number. Mr. Biggles does not buy numbers; he buys comparables. TIDELOCK’s read has to resolve against titles that already returned money, or it is trivia.

07 The four assetsSpine census

The comparable is the asset, and it is already built.

Mr. Biggles pushes his glasses up. Where has that indexed before? A vote on TIDELOCK is worth money only when it resolves against the spine and a title that returned something.

A vote is worth money only when it carries a comparable — when the answer is not “73% liked it” but “this concept indexes where that title indexed, and that title returned this.”

Four assets already stand behind the read: Shiv's Curated Content Catalog (12,955,801 certified rows), the ground truth joined to it, the narrative decoder shared with the sibling HIT Predictor, and a Sample Set of 7,412 titles that solves the cold start.

Every row is licensed or curated. Nothing is taken from elsewhere, so nothing becomes a liability when a buyer asks where it came from. And the demand data compounds: every render, vote and scroll-away is a labelled example nobody else holds. At critical mass the model itself — trained on years of fan behaviour against realised outcomes — is what media buyers pay for.

07 The text-only floorScript Ratings

Text can see the features. It cannot see the audience.

<2%of variance

Six narrative features scored from summary text, on 9,901 audience-covered titles. The features are real — an LLM judge agrees with the heuristic at ρ .39–.57 on four of six — and they explain under 2% of what the audience did. Published anyway.

That is why trailers, not text: show people something watchable and measure behaviour. The text-only result is also the floor P0 must beat, by Δρ ≥ 0.10, published either way.

07 What this is notOur read · Sep 26

Alone in the quadrant that reads behaviour on unmade concepts.

Not a demand tracker for content that already exists (Parrot Analytics). Not a logline concept survey (NRG, MarketCast) — stated preference, n≈400. Not a script-scoring model on text (the StoryFit / ScriptBook generation, including our own pilot). Not a rough-cut screening (Screen Engine, NRG). Not a greenlight financial model (Cinelytic, Largo).

A streamer could render trailers with the same APIs; it cannot see the cross-studio comparable and will not publish its error bar.

07 The ground truth, drawnSpine · 900 of 7,412

Every dot is a released film. This is what a read resolves against.

When Mr. Biggles asks where a concept has indexed before, this is the plane he is asking about — budget against what the world paid back, one point per finished title. TIDELOCK would be resolved into it at P0.

Budget × worldwide gross, log–log, a 900-title sample of the corpus. The amber line is 1× — the film paid for itself; the green line is 10×. 62.8% of the corpus sits above the amber line; 43.3% at least doubled. Big budgets are safer than they look — ≥ $100M recoups 87% of the time at a 2.58× median — and small ones are where the price is wrong most often: $5–30M titles recoup 58% at 1.37×.

That asymmetry is the business. The reads that matter most are on the scripts that cost least to ask about.

08 Three sidesDraft terms

Writers get produced, paid and acknowledged; studios get a price; audiences get a say.

Mara gives one script, non-exclusive, revocable. Mr. Biggles gives slate titles under NDA and 30 minutes a month. Dani gives attention. Each leaves with something priced before the money.

Each side gives something the others cannot supply, and gets a price before the money is spent. Three sides, one clearing, both directions.

Who is the customer? Studios, streamers and buyers pay — for closed panels, signed certificates and the Demand Feed. Writers pay nothing; they get produced. Consumers pay with attention (and, at P1, a subscription) for a say in what gets made. The demand data is what is sold; the produced script is what everyone came for.

Will a writer let the world see the script? No — and they never have to. The script is never shown. The trailer is public, the script stays private, the Demand Index is private by default, and the rights partner co-designs the terms. Incentive, not exposure, is what brings the premium scripts in.

08 The clearingBoth directions

A two-sided market clears in both directions or not at all.

Supply enters at Render — public-domain scripts, loglines, opted-in specs, studio slates under NDA. Demand enters at Vote — attention, replay, scroll-away, head-to-head choice. Both leave with a price — the writer's private Demand Index, the studio's signed certificate, the buyer's option.

The ledger

Say Mr. Biggles’s studio runs its slate through a closed panel. The fee is one line in a ledger. That line is where the company’s revenue starts, and it is deliberately first.

09 Order is the strategyComputed (E)

Panels fund the build. The feed builds the data. The data builds the business.

Mr. Biggles’s slate runs through closed panels from P2; that fee is one line under Panels, and it pays first because his budget line already exists. TIDELOCK’s own line, an option, comes at P3.

Both, sequenced honestly. Panels pay first because the budget line already exists. The feed launches at P1 as the agency product and drops cost per read another order of magnitude. If retention does not hold, recruited and partner audiences keep the panel business alive — dependency and fallback are both on the chart.

Studio Panels · Studios, streamers, prodcos pay · P2Consumer Feed · Viewers, advertisers pay · P1Demand Feed · Strategy, programming, acquisitions pay · P3Option Flow · Buyers pay · P3

Studio Panels: closed NDA testing of a development slate, priced against the replaced screening. Consumer Feed: short-form entertainment with agency — subscription + ads. Demand Feed: standing subscription to aggregate demand by genre, demo, narrative feature, window. Option Flow: brokerage on threshold-clearing concepts; revenue share to writers.

Two of the four engines sell demand data — the certificate and the feed. The fourth is the reason the data exists: option flow is where a priced concept becomes a produced title, and where the writer is paid. A producer can also run it the other way — use the Demand Feed to decide what to make, and be their own proof of concept.

What changed in this version. The plan used to hire a phase’s team on the gate month and sell cold afterwards. Discovery-Driven Planning calls that the dangerous assumption: a venture that needed cash in twelve months had first to recruit a sales force — four months to hire, four to learn, four left to sell. The fix in the case was not a better forecast. It was co-developing the offer with a paying pilot customer, which produced cash “with virtually no sales staff on board.” Two paid pilots now run from month 1, the panel opens at month 10 instead of 13, and each phase’s headcount arrives over nine months rather than on the gate. Break-even moves from month 36 to month 25, and peak cash need from $12.7M to $5.6M.

Not in the model: brand placements inside trailers and produced shorts — a plausible upside line once the feed has an audience, left out until there is a benchmark to cite.

60-month P&L computed from window.PGModel defaults (E) — not a projection · benchmarks named in Sources C · Shiv to correct · sequencing per McGrath & MacMillan, Discovery-Driven Growth ch. 6
09 Two sides of the bookFrom the model (E)

Liquidity arrives in sequence.

Concepts entering each month on the supply side, the audience in the feed on the demand side. Log scale; the lines move with the drivers two steps on.

The gap between them is the constraint the model now enforces. A concept can only be panelled if there is an audience to read it — so panel concepts are capped at feed viewers × reads per viewer ÷ reads per concept, never at what the sales team sold. Instacart’s rule, stated plainly: “we always onboarded supply ahead of demand.” Here the supply is attention. Sell a slate the audience cannot read and the certificate is worthless, which is the failure the cap exists to make visible.

Supply · concepts entering / monthDemand · monthly active audience in the feed
From the model · defaults (E) · P0 calibration concepts, feed catalogue scaling with MAU, panel concepts from P2 capped by available reads · Instacart per SCG-577 Mini Case D
09 How the audience arrivesFrom the model (E)

“How would fans find the trailers to watch initially?”

The question a first reader asked, and the one the whole cost curve turns on. A trailer nobody finds is a render bill. The answer has two halves — what a viewer sees, and where the viewer came from.

What they see. Not a catalogue. The first session asks for a feeling and a few keywords, and the feed ranks against that — the same keyword and feeling machinery running back on §05. Every watch, skip and vote sharpens it. The product is a preference instrument the viewer is willing to feed because feeding it makes their own feed better; the demand data is the exhaust, not the ask.

Where they came from. Four platform launches answer this with numbers rather than intentions, and the model now follows them instead of buying every install:

Paid installs · falls as the loop compoundsReferral · viewer brings viewerOrganic · search, share, free tier

Eventbrite — a free tier is an acquisition channel, not lost revenue: the free loop drove 34% of supply-side awareness and 17% of free creators ran a paid event within twelve months. Here, every trailer page is public and indexable; the paywall sits at agency and depth, not at the door. · GrubHub — solved demand first by putting scraped menus online and letting search do the work, and launched in one Chicago neighbourhood before a second. Here: one genre vertical, indexed title pages, not a national launch. · TaskRabbit — “we spent very little money in the early days on digital ads; paid ads became more important about five years after launch,” with 90%+ of early customers arriving by word of mouth. · Instacart — “about a third of our demand came through referrals early on” and “we did almost no paid marketing early on.”

So paid share is no longer a constant. It starts at 50% of new viewers and decays toward 25% as penetration rises — the single largest cost reduction in the plan, worth five months of break-even on its own. The honest cost of that: a free viewer does not pay on day one either. Paying share now starts at 1.2% and climbs to 3% over twelve months, which makes year one worse, not better. Both corrections belong in the same model.

The counter-example is on the same page. GrubHub reached 19.9M active users and $1.312B of revenue in 2019 — against $1.318B of cost, a $6M operating loss. Audience is not the answer to break-even. Sequencing and margin are.

Acquisition composition computed from the model (E) · discovery mechanics and all quoted figures from Wadhwani, Lubinski & Viebig, “Platform Startups: Launching Online Marketplaces” (SCG-577), Mini Cases A–D · personalised ranking is the §05 instrument, not a new claim
09 Headline driversPick a plan · drag the sliders

The sequencing logic

Panels fund the feed. The feed creates the data. The data creates the licensing business. The licensing business creates the option flow. Reverse that order and you are running a consumer media company with no revenue and no comparables — the failure mode of every script-voting platform that came before.

Three plans, one model. Sales-led is the earlier version of this deck: hire the phase team on the gate, sell cold, buy every install. Pilot-led is the default now. Penguin stall is the downside the cases name — the feed never reaches liquidity, so panels fall back to recruited audiences at $3.00 a read.

Set the requirement at $10M of before-tax profit on a 30% return on sales and run all three through the reverse income statement below. The sales-led plan books more revenue — $32.3M against $31.6M — and still misses by $0.8M, because it spends $23.1M to get there. The pilot-led plan clears at 37.5% return on sales on less revenue. That is the whole argument in one row: this is not a bigger business than the last version. It is the same business, profitable eleven months sooner, on under half the capital.

Switch the plan or drag a slider on the stage · every change re-runs the 60-month model
Reverse income statement · Y5 (McGrath & MacMillan, Table 6-1)

Run upside down: name the profit the venture must earn, apply a required return on sales, and derive the revenue it needs and therefore the cost it is allowed. Then subtract what this model actually spends. What is left is the buffer — and a negative buffer means the plan does not work, however large the market.

Loglines anyone can submit are the engine of the feed.

User-submitted loglines enter under an open intake and a platform licence. This is where virality comes from — and it is noisy, so it needs originality screening and moderation before it meets an audience.

The wave clears into the consumer feed and, in aggregate — by genre, demo and feature — into the Demand Feed. No option flow: a logline is not a script a buyer can option.

The analogue

TIDELOCK has no box office to check against. To learn whether a read means anything, the instrument needs scripts whose endings are already known. 200 of them.

11 Protocol · pre-registeredNot yet run

Nothing gets priced until 200 released titles are back-tested blind — published either way.

TIDELOCK has no ending to check. A released title among the 7,412 does: rendered blind from its logline, read the same way, its gross already known. That is the script's analogue.

Sample at least 200 titles from the 7,412 spine titles with certified budget, gross and synopsis. Render each logline as a concept trailer. Blind the panel: no title, cast or marketing. Compute a Demand Index; correlate it with log(worldwide gross ÷ budget).

Thresholds fixed before the run: the 95% bootstrap interval's lower bound above zero, and the correlation beating a text-only baseline by at least 0.10.

200 sampled titles7,412-title corpus
7,412 = curated_v2.movie_box_office ⋈ movie_master, budget > 0, gross > 0, synopsis > 40 chars · queried 2026-09-01 · Sources B
11 Ghost the outcomeSeeded

Ghost the outcome. Both shapes are drawn before the run so neither can be a surprise.

Pass: the blind Demand Index tracks log(gross ÷ budget) strongly enough that the bootstrap interval clears zero and beats the text-only floor by Δρ ≥ 0.10. Null: the cloud is round, the interval straddles zero, and the number has no price.

Every point on the stage is seeded, not measured; ρ and the interval are computed live from those seeded points. P0 replaces them.

If it holds, the number has a price. If it does not hold, that gets published too.

The gate has two exits and both are public. A pass licenses the certificate. A null retires the claim — and is published with ρ, CI and the text-only baseline, whatever they are.

Precondition before either: ≥ 50 QC-passed renders. The corpus was queried 2026-09-01; no P0 figure appears on this page until the inputs are spine rows and the telemetry is human.

11 The corpus, by yearSpine · 1995–2025

Thirty release years, every one of them measured after the fact.

TIDELOCK’s analogue is somewhere on this line — a released film whose ending is known. The back-test picks 200 of them, renders each from its logline, and asks whether a read at first draft would have known.

Median multiple by release year, with the corpus count behind it. 2019 was the best year on the spine at 2.29×, 72% recouped. 2020 fell to 0.69× and 42%. Both facts arrived the only way the industry ever learns anything about demand: after the film was made, released and counted.

The gate’s question is narrower than the chart: on 200 of these, blind, does the audience’s behaviour on a trailer track log(gross ÷ budget) with a lower confidence bound above zero, and beat text alone by 0.10? If yes, the number has a price. If not, that is published too.

Follow the script

If the gate holds, TIDELOCK gets a number with an interval. Here is what could still make that number wrong, in the order it would happen.

12 Risk 01 · Construct validityUp front

Four ways this fails, stated before anyone trades on it.

TIDELOCK's trailer sells a premise: an ocean on a schedule. The film would be the engineer, the 72 hours and the ending. The gap between them is Risk 01, sized by the back-test.

Premise is not picture. A trailer measures appetite for the premise, not the finished film. The gap between the two is real, and it is the first thing the instrument has to size.

We do: size the gap with the 200-title back-test; sell only where it is measured. We publish: ρ, CI and the text-only baseline, whatever they are.

Risk register · construct validity sized by the §11 back-test · published either way
12 Risk 02 · ConfoundNot yet exercised

A weak render kills a strong script.

A weak take on the Atlantic reads as a weak premise, and TIDELOCK dies at draft for the wrong reason. Same seat, same tier, 8.5 / 10 on five checks, every head-to-head.

The render contaminates the signal: a great premise on a bad take reads as a bad premise. We do: same seat, same tier, same QC bar across every head-to-head — a QC threshold of 8.5 / 10 on five checks, held constant.

We publish: the reject rate from P0. The gate is a specification today; it has not yet been exercised on real renders.

QC gate: specification (8.5/10, five checks); not yet exercised · claude_creative_director_qc · reject rate published from P0 · Sources D
12 Risk 03 · Rights & consentDraft terms

A supply problem, permanently.

Terms done wrong lose the writers — and the strongest signal with them. Nothing in the technology recovers that. We do: draft terms in §10; rights partner co-designs; opt-in training use only.

We publish: the terms, redlined, and the opt-in count.

Writer terms · DRAFT — rights partner to redline · training use OFF by default · §10
12 Risk 04 · AdversarialRed-team at P1

The thumb can be brigaded.

A public vote can be gamed. We do: sell the revealed-preference layer, not the thumb; run a scripted 10k-vote brigade at P1 and watch what the index does.

We publish: index movement under attack and whether it was flagged. The defence is heuristic today; the red-team result is published at P1 — the pass line is an index move of ≤ 3 points with the attack flagged.

P1 red-team: scripted 10k-vote brigade · index moves ≤ 3 points and the attack is flagged · logged as calibration_control · §13

Derived figures and formulas

Per take = seconds × rate. Renders per concept = 3 candidate takes + 1 QC-approved final = 4.

Render cost per read (floor) = (4 × per take) ÷ reads. Loaded cost per read = (render + media + opex) ÷ reads. Defaults (E).

Predicted engagement curve (§04/§05, SPEC): base = NEI × 0.7; hook gaussian μ=2 s; exposition dip μ=9 s; escalation half-sine from 12 s; climax gaussian μ=25 s; cliffhanger ramp after 28.5 s; clamped 0–100 — the illustrative shape of the specified arc, not a model output.

Orders of magnitude = log10($37.50 ÷ loaded cost per read). Three at loaded defaults; render-only is the floor and is shown as an absolute number, never led with.

P&L (window.PGModel, inline): render cost per concept = 3 × 30 s × $0.07 + 1 × 30 s × $0.12 + $0.60 LLM = $10.50; feed MAU on a logistic S-curve; panels = contracts × concepts × price + seat fee; data = enterprise ACV ÷ 12 + Lite; options = take × (fee + exercise × purchase). Sources F · Precedent trailers (TMDB)

Fourteen released titles whose demand was measured before production — or whose trailer was the measurement. Metadata, trailer links and stills from TMDB v3 (/movie/{id}?append_to_response=videos,release_dates, /movie/{id}/keywords, image.tmdb.org w154/w300); thumbnails from YouTube; all embedded as data URIs at build time, no runtime calls. Budget and gross are crowd-sourced on TMDB and unaudited — corroborate with The Numbers before quoting a multiple.
